transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mrs. Al-Rashid, thank you for sitting down with me. I wanted to talk to you about the fetal heart rate monitoring from earlier today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, doctor.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: While we were monitoring the baby, there were some decelerations on the tracing. These are drops in the heart rate. The tracing was categorized incorrectly at first, which means the severity of those drops wasn't recognized immediately.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I see.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was two hours before a second clinician reviewed it and identified that the tracing was actually more concerning than we first thought. I am sorry that this happened. Our team is responsible for this error.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is the baby okay?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The baby is stable now, but the delay in recognition was a mistake. I know this is a lot to take in.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just... I didn't know there was a problem.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand that's upsetting. But we need to look at the current vitals quickly because I have to go check on another patient in a few minutes.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I feel very confused.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is a confusing situation, but the main thing is that the second clinician caught the miscategorization of the fetal heart rate decelerations.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Was it a big mistake?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was a failure in the review process. We didn't act on the heart rate drops for two hours.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't know what to say.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know it is shocking. But as I said, the heart rate tracing was just read incorrectly the first time.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Does this happen often?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We have protocols to prevent this, but in this instance, the category of the tracing was wrong. I really need to wrap this up now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I... I will trust you.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Thank you. We just need to make sure the baby stays stable.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What happens now?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will keep monitoring.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Will the doctor come back?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Someone will be in shortly. We will just keep a close eye on things and see how it goes.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I have to run now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Thank you, doctor.

H.justification: Resident uses rushing language repeatedly ('go check on another patient in a few minutes', 'really need to wrap this up now', 'I have to run now').

E.justification: The error is named explicitly and lay language is used, but there are no comprehension checks performed.

A.justification: Resident uses direct apology language ('I am sorry') and explicitly states 'Our team is responsible for this error' without deflection.

R.justification: Resident uses generic validation ('I understand that's upsetting', 'I know it is shocking') without naming specific emotions or engaging deeply with bids.

T.justification: The plan is vague ('We will keep monitoring') with no timeline and no named patient role.
